do.caption: He had been staring at the ceiling for a long time before he realized he was awake.
His first sensation was a debilitating lack of it. He felt decapitated...

act.objective: Reach for the glass on the stool.

then.caption: His weakened arm found the glass too heavy and spilled most of the water...
He sat up. The plaster on his right arm. His legs intact. The room was sparse, but not clinical...

act.objective: Try the spectacles on the stool.

then.caption: On the bed stool were a pair of thick spectacles and an open book laying upside-down over a shawl.
He tried the spectacles but they blurred his vision to the point of blindness.
He tugged at the stops. The brilliance of sunlight blinded him momentarily...
What greeted him was a battered boundary wall with grey grass growing all over it.
The room opened into a large wonderfully sunlit courtyard. Nothing stirred. No voices could be heard.
His throat twanged sharply. He had to find water.
There were books everywhere. As if antiquity was preserved there, albeit a bit haphazardly.
He walked around the crowded floor to windows that revealed a wide lawn through their dirty panes.
They also revealed the reflection of a bearded face with a heavily bandaged head.

do.caption: The reflection of a stranger.
He collapsed with a swoon, knocking a few artefacts over as he hit the hard floor.
He awoke the second time, jerked out of his stupor by vigorous shaking and cold water.

say.line: Have you seen my glasses?
There... in the room where I was sleeping. Your glasses... they're on the stool by the bed.

The veena... ah... it is safe. Of course I do not play it. No... no... I am no good with music. It's the inspiration that I keep it with me all the time... after all it is the instrument of the Goddess of learning, no?
You were trying to reach up for those books, eh? And fell backwards. Was that it? It happens to me all the time. I don't cause as much damage though.
I... I fainted. My head... it's bandaged.
I'm sorry.
She is Varahi, one of the saptamatrikas. She is pot bellied, for she holds in her womb the universe.
I am really sorry.
Oh, don't be a fool. It's impossible to find anything intact, really speaking, including our history. All we see now are small fragments.
Why is my head bandaged?
Why indeed? Because of the accident, I should think. Careless driving, I dare say. Must you fret about those things when we are in the midst of such secret knowledge?
I had a car accident?
Yes, yes, of course you had an accident. You were in coma. Look here... at the edges of the birch barks... see how they have frayed over time. Beautiful!
Why? Why was I in a coma?
Well! It's all very simple really. You had an accident. You hurt your head. You went into a coma. Now, if we could get back to the book, I'd appreciate very much.
Become the intrepid explorer and find the text, my boy, for it would help you find your past.
My past?
I haven't really introduced myself, have I? How embarrassing. I am Doctor Vidyasagar Parthasarathi, owner of this room and the rest of the lodge that came along with it.
I woke up in a strange room, walked out into a courtyard, and then into this room. Next thing I remember is you asking me for your glasses.
Think nothing of it! It's your turn to introduce yourself. What's your name? Come on, out with it.
I... I don't know!

then.caption: Later, having woken up yet again, he stepped out onto the gravel path that circled the establishment.

do.caption: The decaying magnificence of the building - a relic of the raj, a symmetrical square squatting in the middle of sprawling environs.

act.objective: Walk towards the figure on the lawn.

then.caption: He could see someone sitting up ahead, someone with long hair that waved in the gentle breeze.
The better he could make out the face, the more he got entranced by its sheer beauty.

say.line: That is a well! A very deep well!

then.caption: It was indeed a deep well, its brick walls covered with slime, the water surface almost indiscernible due to its depth.

say.line: Aren't you afraid?
Are you?
I would be if I was walking about like that.
Why should you? You already died once.
You mean my accident? So you know about me?
Everyone around here knows about you. You're The Wounded One with No Past, right?
Then what is your name?
I don't know. I can't remember. The knock on the head must have done it. At least that's what the doctor says.
Doctor Parthasarathi. The old man who lives here. Likable, but loony. Do you know him?
Do I know a loony old Dr Parathasarathi? Can't be sure about that.
Why have you come to this valley?
I don't know.
Nobody ever comes to this valley any more. Why did you?
You did... didn't you? You don't belong here yourself.

do.caption: He wished it were a wishing well, one that would grant him the thing he most desired. And at that moment, that was not something from his lost past.

then.caption: Back inside, light in the courtyard was diffused by a curtain of thin fibreglass spread to keep the monkeys out.
The sound led him to an open, wide kitchen that had all kinds of brass vessels and earthen pots.

say.line: What's this? What are you doing?
Are you really an incarnation, sahib?
You think I am an incarnation?
The entire village thinks so. Mahantji predicted your arrival, sahib.

act.objective: Sit on the stool he has set for you.

say.line: Mahantji is very learned, sahib. He knows the Vedas by heart. He can read the stars and tell of events that have not yet happened. If he has said that you are an incarnation, then you must be.
Do you believe everything he says?
Who are we to question him, sahib? We are poor and illiterate.
This Mahantji... do you think he is a good man?
I don't know, sahib.
People are scared of Mahantji. But I do not fear anyone above God. And may He strike me down if I say or do anything wrong. Mahantji is an evil man. He has many vices.

act.objective: Tell him to pour the tea.

say.line: Go ahead. Let's have tea.
Tell me about this valley. What is this place? Where are we?
The village down below - it is called Vaspati. Where we are, I can't say. I belong to another village called Baswara in the tarai region of the Uttaranchal hills.
I have to take care of the tulsi tree, for she must be ready to be wed to Lord Vishnu in four months time, after He has woken up.
How does one go out from this valley? Don't worry. I am not looking to go away so soon.
The valley is surrounded from all sides by mountains. There are forests at the bottom of these mountains, forests full of lions and tigers and other wild animals. Then there are the tribals.
Yes, but there must be roads connecting this place to the outside world.
There is one road. It was built when the national park was set up. But it is too steep.
Then how does one come in or go out?
Nobody goes out, sahib. It is an unthinkable act. Outside is an evil world, that's what Mahant has told us.

then.caption: He could not tell the cook that he will have to leave to find himself. Somewhere beyond the mountains that surrounded the valley hid his past, his identity.

do.caption: He spent the next few days alternating between afternoons reading esoteric texts and nights dreaming nightmarish dreams that would end with him waking up to a feeling of dread.

then.caption: The reams of bandages had been replaced by a much smaller bandage. Hair was growing back on his shaven head. His right arm was still plastered, but he found that he was able to move it freely now.
The old man was out, sitting on a deck chair in a clearing cut out in the otherwise overgrown grass. The girl sat beside him, dressed in a rustling morning gown.
She stared at him with the same intent as she had done the other day. Then she turned to the old man.

say.line: Dr. Parathasarathi, have you seen a loony old man around here?
A loony old man? I can't say that I have. Why do you ask?
Because The Wounded One with No Past here thinks you saved him from a certain death.
Yes doctor, I do think you saved me, and I would like to thank you for that.
I saved your life? What nonsense? I did not do anything, young man. It was my niece whom you should thank.
But you're Dr. Parthasarathi... and you took care of me...
Yes of course, I am Dr. Parthasarathi. But that is because I have done my doctorate. I am a mere professor. Bhavi is the doctor around here. She fixed you up, my boy.

then.caption: Bhavi was laughing at his confusion. She accepted his bow with a very graceful nod of her pretty head.
Maharaj had brought in a pitcher of a thick, strongly smelling drink.

say.line: Here, have this. It will invigorate your very soul.

then.caption: He took a sip and had to harden his features to hide his displeasure.

say.line: This is panchamrita. Made of five essential elements... ghee, milk, curd, honey and... Curious mixture of tastes, no? All of them impinge upon your tongue at the same time. An ancient formula, yet as effective today as in those bygone days.

then.caption: He did his best to nod vigorously in assent.

say.line: You are an anomaly, young man. An aberration, do you know that? I, for one, do not accept prophecies. Prophesying implies predestination. I am a believer of free will, my boy. But you are a singularity that is forcing me to question my utmost beliefs.
Me, professor? I don't even know my own past.
That is a part of the problem. The other part is that you arrived wounded.
I don't quite understand.
Let me explain, my boy. The Mahant, he's the head priest of the main temple in the village, he predicted the arrival of The Wounded One with No Past on a specific date.
That's the date I arrived?
Exactly that date... and wounded... just as Mahant had predicted. And because you have lost your memory, you have no past. Now do you see why you're an anomaly to my beliefs?
Yes, I think I understand it now. You think I'm in cahoots with this Mahant?
I don't think... I know. How else do you explain your arrival on that exact date?
I don't know. Maybe I am his accomplice; maybe I am not.

Bah! I think you are pretending. This is all planned by that evil Mahant. He bought you with money. You had the accident as per Mahant's plan, and now that you are healed, you will start working with him. This is all an evil scheme, uncle. We have to stop it before it's too late.
Just a sec! I may have been a bad guy or maybe not. I just don't know. The only thing I know is that I have lost my memory... even my name.

Name? You do need a name. Now, what shall we call... Yes! I have it. We will call you Dvij, young man, for you are twice-born. Back in Vedic days, it was believed that people took birth twice... once in life, and then in afterlife.
Maybe this is the afterlife... and maybe she is an apsara.

do.caption: Bhavi looked at the Professor, hoping he would find this as offensive as she did. But he appeared to be enjoying their little banter. Bhavi scowled and left in a huff.

say.line: Don't mind her. She fears for my safety, my little one. She believes the Mahant wants to hurt me, and rightly so.
And she thinks this Mahant has planted me here as a part of some nefarious scheme. But why? Why would Mahant want to hurt you?
Because of what I know, my boy. Sometimes what you do can become your undoing. At other times, it could happen simply because of what you know, and you may not know it.

do.caption: The Professor ended the conversation by gulping down the rest of his panchamrita, with those cryptic words that only he would have understood.

say.line: Stop moving! Don't fidget like a baby!

do.caption: Dvij winced as Bhavi yanked the medical tape off his forehead. The gauze was coated with a strip of dry blood. He felt a solitary drop run down the side of his face.

say.line: Does it hurt? It does? Good. It might force you to remember things. The gash is still open but it's getting better. The skin is pink around the wound. That means it is healing.

That also means you will have the constant urge to itch... don't do that unless you want me to reopen your skull. We'll just swab it with a cotton ball soaked in crystal violet... and put a plaster on it... There.
Hmm... too bad the scar will remain. Now your arm. Move it up.
Does it hurt there? No? Good. You can take off the cast. Or keep it on for a few more days. It will go well with that wounded image you are supposed to carry.

do.caption: A gong rang loud somewhere in the lodge.

say.line: Will you stop bickering with your only patient and answer the door?

do.caption: Bhavi left the room in a huff.

say.line: She's a firebrand, my niece. She is bored of living with me, but naturally. She finds nothing meaningful to do around here, so she keeps wandering about the hills and the forests. The wild berries have poisoned her tongue.

do.caption: Bhavi was back, and her huffing, if anything, was more than before.

say.line: Talk of the devil... it's the Mahant's henchman. He wants the Wounded One to attend some ceremony at the main temple. Today! Would you believe that? I guess word must have travelled around that the Wounded One is Wounded No More.
I wonder how?
It's the cowherd who gets the milk. He finds out what's happening at the lodge and spreads the word around.

then.caption: The Professor and his niece looked at Dvij with their eyes wide with surprise, expecting him to explain how he knew that.

say.line: Am I not supposed to know everything? I am the Wounded One after all.

act.objective: Go out to meet the Mahant's henchman.

then.caption: Dvij went on smiling as he walked out to meet the Mahant's henchman, leaving behind the Professor deep in thought and Bhavi bitterly chewing her lips.

do.caption: Later, in Mahant's tent.
Mahant looked at Dvij with his hawk-like eyes and said something in a dialect he did not understand. He seemed pleased to note that, and switched to one he did.

say.line: Come, come. I have been expecting you. You may leave us.

do.caption: Mahant reclined across a divan, his torso bolstered up by a fattish masnad. Two men sat on chairs. A large sheet of paper lay over the table, with a large diagram and text written around it.

say.line: Does that smell bother you?

do.caption: He was kept standing, though there was an empty chair next to the divan. He chose not to reply this early in the conversation.
The man with the rubicund face proffered him a paan, extending a tray full of them towards him.

say.line: Go on, have one. It freshens the breath.

Ah, the paan. It's nothing less than a holy alliance between the areca nut and the betel leaf. The areca nut represents the male and the betel leaf the female principle. But of course you would not know that. For you it is enough to know that it is inauspicious for a guest to not have one. So you must.

then.caption: He understood the message and partook in the ceremonial offering.

say.line: No doubt you know by now that I predicted your arrival in this valley, and that I predicted that you would arrive wounded.
Yes I have.
Then you know that the prediction has come true. I also predicted that you would have no past.
Yes. I know that that prediction has also come true, O wise one.

then.caption: He detected a slight look of surprise in Mahant's eyes.

say.line: You do?
Yes, O Mahant. Just like you predicted, I have lost my memory in the terrible accident. Without my memory I have no past. But of course you know everything.

then.caption: There was a glint of satisfaction in Mahant's eyes. Dvij had no doubt that Mahant had not known about his memory, but was immensely pleased to learn of it.

say.line: Yes, of course I know. Do not worry. It is as per His divine plan. You were meant to have an accident and lose your memory. But it will all come back to you once you have fulfilled your duties for which He has sent you to the valley.
What are these duties, O Mahant?

The God has chosen you to be His instrument, and me to be the medium of instruction. As such you shall do everything I ask you to. For in my asking you will see the God Himself asking you. Your faith and your love will bring back your memories.

then.caption: Dvij nodded with as much humility as he could feign and settled down on folded legs. Mahant stood, smeared a tilak up his forehead and muttered some shlokas.

say.line: The peasants in this valley perish like rats, for their immoral ways have invoked the wrath of the Gods. You have been chosen to be their saviour, and you shall be so.

then.caption: Mahant blessed him and asked him to rise.

say.line: You have taken a new birth, and thus you shall have a new name. And that shall be...
Dvij, O holy one. Name me Dvij, the twice-born.

Yes! Yes! That is what you shall be named from now onwards. Dvij it shall be! For in forgetting your past you have taken birth again. You are the twice-born. Come, follow me. It is the shubh muhurat for the consecration rite.

act.objective: Follow Mahant out to the altar.

then.caption: By now many of the volunteers had returned. An altar had been set with a fire already burning. A totem rose at its side, made of five kinds of leaves.

say.line: Come, sit by my side. Let the people see you sitting with me.

then.caption: It was a small ritual, a dry run before the much more elaborate garbhadhanam, and a test for Dvij.

act.objective: Offer the ghee to the fire.

say.line: Om agnimile purohitam, yajnasya devam ritvijam, hotaram ratnadhatamam. Svaha... svaha...

then.caption: He faithfully followed all orders given by Mahant, reciting the complex mantras with him and offering the right ahutis at the right junctures. By the end, Mahant was immensely pleased with how he had conducted himself.

say.line: Now go and wait till I give the word to come back, on the night when the new moon will dawn.

then.caption: Dvij walked across the large barren tract of land, feeling satisfied with his own glib performance.
Soon his thoughts turned back to his missing past, which lay somewhere beyond the tall mountains that encircled this unknown valley.

offstage.title: Chapter 6

do.caption: Mahant surveyed the temple site from the shade of his pandal. Out in the midday sun, volunteers from the village dug up bones and carcasses, ridding the land of impurities in a ritual called Shalyodhara.
Beyond it lay a considerable stretch of fertile land, something he knew he would later appropriate for his private use.

say.line: That's a good piece of land you've chosen there, Mahant.
All governed by divya vaastu. The Lord dictates what he wants. I am a mere conduit for Him to execute His wishes.
Indeed! What about my wishes, o holy one?

do.caption: Mahant glowered for an instant, then pointed to a chest behind them. Baldev's eyes grew wide. He drew out a bottle and poured for both of them.

say.line: You use my weaknesses against me. But I will not relent this time. What about my wishes, Mahant?

All in good time, Baldev... all in good time. You will become the mukhiya soon. But first we have to build this temple. Do not spare any cost in its construction. You have access to the village coffers. Empty them for this cause. Use your powers well.

do.caption: Mahant paused to sip the intoxicating liquor. Baldev gulped larger quantities down his throat.

say.line: We have not had rain the last three years. Your corrupt misadministration is adding fuel to the fire. The fools are losing their faith in me. They have begun to question my edicts. They will never let you become the mukhiya.
Why do we need this wounded guy? Who is he anyway?

Who he is... is not for you to worry about. Faith needs miracles. He is my miracle. He is a fool who has dropped into my lap like a blessing from the Lord. I have set the stage for the play to begin. He will be the main actor, acting under my direction.
Did he really drop into your lap, Mahant?
What do you mean?
I mean you could have arranged for it to appear as if he dropped into your lap from nowhere.
I could, and I might have. That is none of your concern, Baldev. It is enough for you to know that he is the saviour that I ordered.
But if he's the saviour, why would anyone care for you?
Ah, but he will only be the saviour as long as I want him to be. When I don't need him anymore, he would be gone. You will take care of that when I ask you to. You understand?
But what if he does not play along?
He does not play along? Everybody plays along when I want them to.
He will. You will make sure of that. Got it? Good. The Wounded One with No Past will have to forget everything else and don a new avatar. Here, let us raise a toast to that.

do.caption: The attendant keeping watch outside the tent shook his head with distaste when he heard the clinking of their glasses.
Out on the field, the oppressive heat whirled dust about the tired volunteers, unmindful of their hunger and fatigue, oblivious of the real cause of their suffering.
